1) Budgetary concerns. Maintaining a full-time paid department for an area that has a minimal amount of fires (under 10, for example) per year is a waste of taxpayer funds. Unlike law enforcement officers, who can take a proactive role in public safety in addition to reactive responses, fire departments are almost entirely reactive. Meaning if there's no fire, they're spending their shift at the fire station (possibly training or maintaining equipment, but more likely not). With volunteers, the community saves a great deal of money by not staffing a fire station 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

2) Training. Though it may vary by region, in my area all volunteer firefighters are required to have the same training and certifications as paid firefighters. Volunteers can be dismissed if they are not up to standard, fail to respond to fire calls, and many other infractions that paid firefighters are subject to. While their professionalism may be lacking compared to their paid counterparts, they can be just as capable. Also keep in mind that, unlike some paid emergency responders who take the job simply for the money/prestige/power/etc or have no better options, volunteers typically sign up because they want to help their community.

3) Quality of life. Being a paid, full-time firefighter is a serious commitment. They are often required to work long rotating shifts and may have to maintain residence at the fire station. This, coupled with the stress of the job if particularly active, can be tough on home life, affecting time spent with family. There can also be restrictions on personal conduct, appearance, and such. Many are not willing to make that sacrifice. Volunteer departments allow individuals to greatly lessen the impact. Liken it to a reserve military service: full-time military service places a great deal of stress on service members and their families, but joining the reserves allows them to still serve in a generally more relaxed environment, with less intrusion on their personal lives, and only have to respond when needed.

First there's the problem of whether the individual seeking euthanasia has the proper capacity to make that decision. Does their condition affect their judgment? For instance, if someone with an inoperable brain tumor or a mental illness wishes to be euthanized, one could argue that their condition has compromised their mental faculties and altered their thought processes. Or if their fear and desperation have influenced their decision-making, leading them to act more on emotion rather than logic. Individuals facing impending pain and death will undoubtedly experience depression, perhaps severely: is that alteration in brain chemistry enough to inhibit or influence their judgment?

Then you have the issue of legal actions and financial implications. Does a next of kin, who strongly opposes euthanasia, believe that the medical professional unduly influenced their loved one’s decision to end their life? This could lead to a lawsuit. Most (if not all) life insurance policies typically do not cover cases of suicide, including assisted suicide - and that is unlikely to change as it opens up significant potential for fraud and abuse. Additionally, there is the possibility of coercion: perhaps from exhausted or self-interested family members who wish to expedite receiving an inheritance or are simply tired of being "burdened" by their dying relative.

Lastly, consider the emotional stress it can place on families. Imagine the conflict between a spouse, who supported their partner's decision to be euthanized, and their child, who vehemently opposed it. Or the lasting negative impression a child may have of a parent - that the parent chose to give up on life rather than fight for every last moment? Or when someone decides, with full family support, to end their life, only for a new treatment or even a cure to be discovered shortly after their death... that decision would be haunting for the survivors.
